text: Scene 1 — Open (0:00–1:00)
theme

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Hello, William. Hello, Alex. Are you tucked in? Good. Pull the blanket up to your chin, because tonight we are going on a very long trip, across a whole ocean, and back almost four hundred years.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: This is "Lambert Lake," the story of your family, told one night at a time. Episode one: "The Boy from Boulogne."
Scene 2 — A boy by the sea, imagined (1:00–4:00)
waves on a stone harbor wall, gulls, a town bell far off

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A long, long time ago, in a country called France, a baby boy was born. His name was Eustache. Eustache Lambert. That's a funny name, isn't it? Say it with me. Oo-stash. Eustache Lambert.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He was born about the year sixteen seventeen, near a place called Boulogne. Now, here is something true about stories this old: we don't know everything. There is a Boulogne by the sea, with a stone wall all the way around it. And there is a little village called Boulogne out among the fields. Nobody knows for sure which one was his. So tonight, let's imagine it was the one by the sea. We'll pretend together, and I'll tell you when we're pretending.
gulls: gulls crying over the water

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Maybe little Eustache liked to run along the harbor wall and watch the fishing boats come in. Maybe his mother called him home for supper.

speaker: MAMAN
text: Eustache! Eustache! Come in, the soup is getting cold!

speaker: YOUNG EUSTACHE
text: One more boat, Maman! There's a big one coming in!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Did you hear that word? Maman. Let's hear how it really sounds in French.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Maman.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Maman means Mom. And Dad, in French, is papa. Almost the same as English.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Papa.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the great big salty sea, where all the boats come from, is la mer.

speaker: FRENCH
text: La mer.

speaker: YOUNG EUSTACHE
text: Maman, where do the big boats go?

speaker: MAMAN
text: Far away, mon petit. Across la mer, to the end of the world.

speaker: YOUNG EUSTACHE
text: I'm going to go there. When I'm big.

speaker: MAMAN
text: When you're big, you can go wherever you like. Tonight, you're going to bed.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now here's something we know for sure, and it might surprise you. Eustache never learned to read or write. Most children in those days never went to school at all. When Eustache grew up and had to sign his name on important papers, he couldn't write it. So he drew a little mark instead. His own special mark.
Scene 3 — The little books from Paris (4:00–6:00)
a stone church, people settling, a quiet cough

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But Eustache could listen. And in those days, there were little books coming out of the city of Paris every year, full of stories from a faraway land called New France. Today we call it Canada.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The books were written by priests called Jesuits, who had gone across the ocean to live and teach there. A priest might read them out loud to a whole room full of people. We don't know if Eustache ever heard one. But let's imagine he did.

speaker: JESUIT
text: "In New France, the rivers are so wide you cannot see the other side. The forests go on forever. And far to the west, beyond the great lakes, live the Wendat people, in long houses made of bark, beside fields of corn."

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Rivers so wide you can't see across! Forests that go on forever! If you were a young man who had never been farther than the next town, wouldn't you want to see that?

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: Father, the men who go to help you over there. What do they do?

speaker: JESUIT
text: Everything, my son. They paddle canoes and carry packs. They build houses and plant corn. They cook and fish and hunt. They take care of the sick. It is hard work, and it is far from home.

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: And what do you pay them?

speaker: JESUIT
text: Nothing at all. Their food. Their clothes. A place to sleep. And a promise that we will look after them as long as they live.
Scene 4 — What a donné was (6:00–7:45)
a hearth fire crackling

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now I'm going to teach you a word that is very important in our story. The word is donné. It sounds like doh-nay.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Donné.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Donné means "given." A donné was a man who gave himself to help the missions. Not for a year. Not for money. For his whole life. He wasn't a priest. He was a helper, a worker, a man who could do a little of everything.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Jesuits started taking donnés in the year sixteen thirty-nine. They needed men who could farm, and build, and hunt, and paddle. And one of the priests wrote something kind about them. He said it didn't seem fair that young men in the flower of their youth would give themselves to such a hard country with so little promised in return.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And Eustache Lambert became one of those men. When he was a grown man, about twenty-five years old, Eustache gave himself to the missions. He became a donné.

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: I can't read. I can't write. But I can carry. I can paddle. I can chop wood all day long. And I can learn. Take me with you.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: We don't know exactly when he sailed. One writer who wrote a book about him thinks it was in the year sixteen forty-four. So let's say good-bye to France, and go down to the harbor. The ship is waiting.
Scene 5 — The crossing (7:45–10:45)
open ocean, a wooden ship creaking, wind in the rigging, big slow waves
creak: the hull and the mast groaning as the ship rolls

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Today, if you flew across the ocean in an airplane, it would take about seven hours. A movie, a snack, a nap, and you're there.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In Eustache's time, it took months. A ship with sails had to wait for the wind. One famous ship in those days left France at the beginning of May, and didn't reach Quebec until the first day of August. Count it on your fingers. May, June, July. Three whole months at sea.

speaker: SAILOR
text: Hold on to something, landsman! Here comes a big one!
waves: a big wave breaks against the hull, spray hissing

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: I'm holding! I'm holding! Is it always like this?

speaker: SAILOR
text: Only on the days that end in "day." You'll get your sea legs. Or you'll get very good at hanging over the side.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Sailors in those days ate hard dry biscuits, and salty meat from a barrel, and drank water that got a little greener every week. When the wind blew, the ship rocked up, and down, and up, and down. And when there was no wind at all, the ship just sat there, still, on a flat blue sea, and everybody waited.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So here is our first big question. And I want you to really think about it. If you were going on a ship for two or three months, across the whole ocean, and you could only take one small bag, what would you pack?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A warm blanket? Your favorite stuffed animal? A ball, for the long, slow days? Think about it. You can tell your dad in the morning.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: We don't know what Eustache packed. Maybe a warm coat. A knife. A wooden spoon. Maybe something small from home, to hold on to.
a calm night at sea, the ship creaking gently, small waves

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Let's imagine one night out on the ocean, halfway across. The wind is soft. The ship creaks, slow and sleepy. And Eustache can't sleep, so he goes up on deck.

speaker: SAILOR
text: Can't sleep, landsman? Come here. I'll show you something. Look up.

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: Stars. More stars than I've ever seen.

speaker: SAILOR
text: Out here there's nothing to hide them. Now, see those seven bright ones, shaped like a big spoon? Follow the two at the end of the spoon, straight up, and you'll find one star all by itself. That's the North Star. It never moves. Every other star goes round and round it all night, but that one stays put. That's how a sailor knows where north is, even in the middle of the ocean.

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: So if I'm ever lost, I look for the spoon, and then the star.

speaker: SAILOR
text: That's it. And here's another secret. Every ship has a cat. Ours is asleep on the rope pile over there. She catches the mice that try to eat our biscuits. Best sailor on the ship. Never gets seasick.
laugh: Eustache and the sailor laughing quietly

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The cat is imagined. But lots of ships really did carry cats, to catch the mice. And sailors really did find their way by the North Star. You can find it too, on a clear night. Look for the big spoon. Ask your dad to show you.
open ocean, morning, gulls far off
gulls: gulls, far off, then closer

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And then one day, after weeks and weeks of nothing but water, the sailors saw birds. Birds mean land is near.

speaker: SAILOR
text: Land! Land ho! That's the mouth of the great river. Another week, and we'll see Quebec.
Scene 6 — Quebec (10:45–12:45)
a wide river, water against the shore, gulls, wind

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The river was the St. Lawrence. And it was so wide at first that you really couldn't see across it, just like the little books said. Slowly it got narrower, and the forests came close on both sides, dark green and endless.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And then, there it was. Quebec. A big rock cliff above the river, with a little fort on top, and a few wooden buildings down by the water. There was a school run by the Jesuits, and a convent where nuns taught girls, and a little hospital. That was the whole town. About as many people as go to a big school today. Just a few hundred.
bell: a small church bell ringing on the cliff above, across the water

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: That's it? That's Quebec?

speaker: JESUIT
text: That's it. Welcome to New France, Eustache.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: When people met each other in Quebec, they said the same thing people in France said. Bonjour.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Bonjour.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Bonjour means good day, or hello. And when somebody helps you carry your heavy bag off the ship, you say merci.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Merci.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Merci means thank you. Bonjour, merci. Hello, thank you. With those two words, you can make a friend almost anywhere.

speaker: EUSTACHE
text: Bonjour, Quebec! Merci, sailors! Merci, ship! Merci, solid ground that doesn't move!
laugh: Eustache and the sailor laughing together

speaker: JESUIT
text: Rest tonight. Next summer, when the canoes come down from the west, you'll go back up the river with them. All the way to the Wendat country. To a mission called Sainte-Marie.
Scene 7 — Goodnight (12:45–14:30)
a quiet summer night by the river, crickets, an owl far off
lullaby

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So that night, Eustache Lambert lay down on solid ground, in a brand new country, for the very first time. Maybe he could still feel the ship rocking, the way you sometimes still feel the waves after a day at the beach.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He was far from Maman. Far from Papa. Far from la mer and the harbor wall. But he was where he wanted to be.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And here's the most amazing part. Eustache Lambert is your grandpa. Your great, great, great, great, great, great, great, great, great, great grandpa. That's a lot of greats. So many greats that we'll have to count them some other night.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Next time, Eustache goes up the river in a birchbark canoe, to a place in the forest called Sainte-Marie. But that's for tomorrow.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Tonight, close your eyes. Feel the ship rocking, slow and gentle. Up, and down. Up, and down. Hear the river outside, going by in the dark.

speaker: FRENCH
text: Bonne nuit.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Bonne nuit means good night. Goodnight, William. Goodnight, Alex. Goodnight, from the shore of Lambert Lake.
